With all of the recent changes, we can now define a points-to connective in the usual Iris way. Great work to all the recent contributors! 

/- Parameterize by a type of UFractions. This example also shows how to deal with this
   kind of polymorphism, which can be tricky. -/
variable {F} [UFraction F]

/- Define an OFunctor for the heap. -/
abbrev F1 : OFunctorPre := constOF <| HeapView F Nat (Agree (LeibnizO String)) AssocList

/- Our OFunctor is present in the global list of OFunctors. -/
variable {GF} [ElemG GF (F1 (F := F))]

/- Allow the types of GF and F, and the UFraction instance for F, to be inferred by γ
   alone. Doing it this way allows us to define a notation for the points-to that does not
   require explicit type parameters. Curiously, I don't need to instantiate this; having it
   in the context is enough for typeclass inference to make this shortcut. I sort of doubt
   that we would want to do this globally for ElemG, but I'm not sure about that. -/
set_option synthInstance.checkSynthOrder false in
class abbrev HasPointsToF1 (γ : GName) (GF : outParam _) (F : outParam (Type _)) [UFraction F] :=
  ElemG GF (F1 (F := F))

/- Define notation for the heap. -/
def points_to (γ : GName) [HasPointsToF1 γ GF F] (k : Nat) (v : String) :=
  iOwn (GF := GF) (F := F1 (F := F)) γ (Frag k (own one) (toAgree ⟨v⟩))

notation k:50 " ↦[" γ:50 "] " v:50 => points_to γ k v

/- In this example, we assume that the setup is complete and a GName has already been
   allocated. -/
example {γ : GName} : 5 ↦[γ] "A" ∗ 5 ↦[γ] "B" ⊢ False := by
  refine iOwn_op.mpr.trans ?_
  refine iOwn_cmraValid.trans ?_
  refine (UPred.cmraValid_elim _).trans ?_
  iintro %H
  have _ := dist_inj <| toAgree_op_validN_iff_dist.mp <|
    (frag_op_validN_iff.mp H).2
  grind

One more thing to show off: an example of defining a weakest precondition, and proving some proof rules with it. The code is still a little rough around the edges but it works! 

 /-! Example: a typical step-indexed weakest precondition -/
section Example3
open OFE

/- In this example, we are given a type of expressions and a type of states, as well as a
   single-stepping function from an operational semantics. -/
class OperationalSemantics (Expr State Value : Type _) where
  step : Expr × State → Expr × State
  to_value : Expr → Option Value
export OperationalSemantics (step to_value)
variable (Expr State Value : Type _) [OperationalSemantics Expr State Value]

/- Let's say that we are also given two OFunctors, and an interpretation of the state into
   state using these resources. -/
variable (F3 F4 : OFunctorPre) [RFunctorContractive F3] [RFunctorContractive F4]
variable {GF} [ElemG GF F3] [ElemG GF F4]
class StateInterpretation (State : Type _) (GF : BundledGFunctors) where
  state_interp : State → IProp GF
export StateInterpretation (state_interp)
variable [StateInterpretation State GF]

/- Again, doing this trick so that we can write WP notations that don't explicitly include
   Expr State and Value. -/
set_option synthInstance.checkSynthOrder false in
class abbrev Ex3WP {Expr : Type _} {State Value : outParam (Type _)} {GF : outParam BundledGFunctors} :=
  OperationalSemantics Expr State Value,
  StateInterpretation State GF

/- Now, we can define a contractive functor for the weakest precondition. -/
def wp_F (wp : Expr → (Value → IProp GF) → IProp GF) (e : Expr) (Φ : Value → IProp GF) :
    IProp GF := iprop(
  (∃ v : Value, ⌜@to_value _ State _ _ e = some v⌝ ∗ |==> Φ v) ∨
  ∀ s, @state_interp State _ _ s -∗
    ∃ e' s', ⌜@step _ _ Value _ (e, s) = (e', s') ⌝ ∗ ▷ |==> (@state_interp _ _ _  s' ∗ wp e' Φ))

instance wp_F_contractive : Contractive (@wp_F Expr State Value _ GF _) where
  distLater_dist {n x y HL} e Φ := by
    refine or_ne.ne (.of_eq rfl) ?_
    refine forall_ne (fun _ => ?_)
    refine wand_ne.ne (.of_eq rfl) ?_
    refine exists_ne (fun v => ?_)
    refine exists_ne (fun _ => ?_)
    refine sep_ne.ne (.of_eq rfl) ?_
    refine Contractive.distLater_dist fun m Hm => ?_
    refine BIUpdate.bupd_ne.ne ?_
    refine sep_ne.ne (.of_eq rfl) ?_
    exact HL m Hm v Φ

def wp {Expr State Value : Type _} [@Ex3WP Expr State Value GF] (e : Expr) (Φ : Value → IProp GF) : IProp GF :=
  (fixpoint <| @wp_F Expr State Value _ GF _) e Φ

theorem wp_unfold (e : Expr) (Φ : Value → IProp GF) :
    wp e Φ ≡ iprop(
        (∃ v : Value, ⌜@to_value _ State _ _ e = some v⌝ ∗ |==> Φ v) ∨
        ∀ s, @state_interp State _ _ s -∗
          ∃ e' s', ⌜@step _ _ Value _ (e, s) = (e', s') ⌝ ∗
          ▷ |==> (@state_interp _ _ _  s' ∗ wp e' Φ)) := by
  apply fixpoint_unfold (f := ⟨(@wp_F Expr State Value _ GF _),
                                @OFE.ne_of_contractive _ _ _ _ (@wp_F Expr State Value _ GF _) _⟩)

/- Now, we can derive some example proof rules. First let's prove a rule for pure deterministic steps: -/
example (e e' : Expr) Φ (Hstep : ∀ {s : State}, @step _ _ Value _ (e, s) = (e', s)) :
    wp e' Φ ⊢ wp e Φ := by
  refine .trans ?_ (equiv_iff.mp (@wp_unfold Expr State Value _ GF _ _ _).symm).mp
  iintro Hspec
  iright
  iintro %s Hs
  iexists e', s
  isplitr
  · ipure_intro
    exact Hstep
  · refine .trans ?_ later_intro      -- FIXME: once iNext is implemented
    refine .trans ?_ BIUpdate.intro   -- FIXME: once iModIntro is implemented
    iintro ⟨Hspec, Hs⟩
    isplitl [Hs]
    · iexact Hs
    · iexact Hspec

/- The pattern of rules for stateful steps, for example, writing to a piece of memory.
   This style of rule applies when ownership over a resource P (eg. k ↦[γ] v) ensures that the state
   can step the expression e to some new expression e', and can be updated to a new resource P'
   in the stepped-to state.
   Then, it suffies to have access to P, and show that access to P' is enough to verify e'. -/
example (e e' : Expr) (P P' : IProp GF) Φ
      (Hstep : ∀ s, iprop(P ∗ @state_interp State GF _ s ⊢ ∃ s',
          ⌜@step _ _ Value _ (e, s) = (e', s')⌝ ∗ |==> (P' ∗ @state_interp State GF _ s'))) :
    P ∗ (P' -∗ wp e' Φ) ⊢ wp e Φ := by
  refine .trans ?_ (equiv_iff.mp (@wp_unfold Expr State Value _ GF _ _ _).symm).mp
  iintro ⟨HP, Hspec⟩
  iright
  iintro %s Hs
  istop -- FIXME: iHave bug?
  refine .trans (sep_mono (sep_mono (wand_intro (Hstep s)) .rfl) .rfl) ?_
  iintro ⟨⟨Hcont, Hspec⟩, HP⟩
  icases Hcont $$ HP with ⟨%s', %Hstep, Hupd⟩
  iexists e', s'
  isplitr
  · ipure_intro; exact Hstep
  refine .trans ?_ later_intro   -- FIXME: once iNext is implemented
  refine .trans bupd_frame_l ?_  -- FIXME: once iMod is implemented
  refine BIUpdate.mono ?_        -- FIXME: once iMod is implemented
  iintro ⟨Hspec, HP', Hs⟩
  isplitl [Hs]
  · iexact Hs
  · iapply Hspec $$ HP'

end Example3
Improvements to these examples are very welcome, by the way

Example proof rule for infinitely looping programs, using Löb induction

/- Looping programs, by Löb induction -/
example (e : Expr) Φ (Hloop : ∀ σ : State, step Value (e, σ) = (e, σ)) :
    ⊢ wp e Φ := by
  iapply BILoeb.loeb_weak
  iintro HLöb
  iapply wp_unfold
  iright
  iintro %s Hs
  iexists e, s
  isplitr
  · ipure_intro; exact Hloop s
  iintro !> !>
  isplitl [Hs]
  · iassumption
  · iassumption
  · exact true_intro

Today after reviewing Sergei's invariants PR I turned my LLM-du-jour towards porting Approxis, a ReLoC style relational logic for probabilistic programs (ie. with a ghost resource representing the spec program). I'd already done a lot of the basic groundwork like the language definition and couplings, today the LLM was able to take the next step and port the weakest precondition and a good handful of its basic lemmas with essentially no input from me.

Glancing through a couple of the proofs I don't see any Iris code that looks unexpected, even if they are a little rough around the edges in their unreviewed form. I think the fact I clanked this out with basically no supervision really speaks to the hypothesis that porting projects inside of Iris is going to be way less work than porting the framework itself.

Here's the definition of the weakest precondition, to give you an idea of the level of complexity we can expect to handle now. It's just plain Iris! Great work to everyone for all the recent PR's, and please feel welcome to share your projects here as well!! 

abbrev wpPre (wp : CoPset → Exp → (Val → IProp GF) → IProp GF) (E : CoPset) (e₁ : Exp) (Φ : Val → IProp GF) : IProp GF :=
  iprop(∀ (σ₁ : State) (e₁' : Exp) (σ₁' : State) (ε₁ : ENNReal),
    (stateInterp σ₁ ∗ SpecUpdateGS.specInterp ⟨e₁', σ₁'⟩ ∗ errInterp ε₁) -∗
      |={E, ∅}=> specCoupl ∅ σ₁ e₁' σ₁' ε₁ (fun σ₂ ρ' ε₂ =>
        match e₁.toVal? with
        | some v => iprop(|={∅, E}=>
            stateInterp σ₂ ∗ SpecUpdateGS.specInterp ρ' ∗ errInterp ε₂ ∗ Φ v)
        | none => progCoupl e₁ σ₂ ρ'.expr ρ'.state ε₂ (fun e₃ σ₃ e₃' σ₃' ε₃ =>
            iprop(▷ specCoupl ∅ σ₃ e₃' σ₃' ε₃ (fun σ₄ ρ'' ε₄ =>
              iprop(|={∅, E}=>
                stateInterp σ₄ ∗ SpecUpdateGS.specInterp ρ'' ∗ errInterp ε₄ ∗
                  wp E e₃ Φ))))))

Example aside, this was a test to see if we could construct an actual BundledGFunctors model, and it and exposed some issues iris-lean#371. The model construction is here, and the (shitty) example code is here. If anyone has any thoughts on the issue please feel free to weigh in.

Posting another win (why am I the only one posting wins here, you folks should brag too!) I was finally able to generalize Metrology beyond discrete probability spaces and into measure spaces.

Backstory: this was the reason I got interested in Iris-Lean in the first place. I spent like 8 months working on this generalization in Rocq and eventually gave up in anger. The fundamental issue was competing hierarchies of canonical structures: I found that specifying that the type of expressions in a language to be both an Iris ofe and a mathcomp-analysis measurable type to be virtually impossible without one of the hierarchies falling apart.

Our typeclasses-based approach in Iris-Lean made this a complete non-issue! In just a couple hours of work, I was able to push past this blocker and bring my dead project back to life :)

I wanted to announce that the mechanisation of Core Lilac by Li et al., 2023, is near complete. Here is on github. Its novel for being one of the few (only??) mechanisation of a probabilistic separation logic with support for continuous distributions. It is built on iris-lean.
I don't have any flashy examples, and there are still some sorries, but the soundness of this simple example is complete.
This is the version of the code from the paper (much more readable, I am yet to figure out how to make things clean)

namespace Unif2

abbrev unif2 : Term [] (Ty.prod .real .real).G :=
  unif01.bind (
  unif01.bind (
  ret (pair (var (tail head)) (var head))
))

notation:10 D ".ₘ1" => (measurableFun_fst ∘ᵣ D)
notation:10 D ".ₘ2" => (measurableFun_snd ∘ᵣ D)

abbrev post2 : LProp := wp (unif2.den ∘ᵣ nil) (λ (Z : RV ⟪Ty.prod .real .real⟫) ↦
  iprop((Z.ₘ1) ∼ unif01_sem ∗ (Z.ₘ2) ∼ unif01_sem))

lemma hrw2₁ {A : Ty} (X Y : RV ⟪A⟫) : (measurableFun_fst ∘ᵣ ((var head.tail).pair (var head)).den ∘ᵣ (Y ;; X ;; nil)) = X := by rfl
lemma hrw2₂ {A : Ty} (X Y : RV ⟪A⟫) : (measurableFun_snd ∘ᵣ ((var head.tail).pair (var head)).den ∘ᵣ (Y ;; X ;; nil)) = Y := by rfl

theorem unif2_spec : iprop(⊢ post2) := by
  rw [post2]
  iintro
  iapply wp_bind
  iapply wp_unif
  iintro %X HX
  iapply wp_bind
  iapply wp_unif
  iintro %Y HY
  iapply wp_ret
  rw [hrw2₁, hrw2₂]
  isplitl [HX]
  · iexact HX
  · iexact HY

end Unif2

A preliminary version of the Iris completeness framework (based on this draft paper by Hostert et al.) has been ported to Iris-Lean and will now be starting cleanup and review!

Completeness is a workhorse theorem for integrating Iris-Lean with other program verification projects:

  • Complete logics can exit an Iris proof in the middle, and prove facts using any external solver. This can be a "manual" proof using techniques from the literature, or an auto-generated proof, or even a proof by way of the soundness theorem of a completely independent program logic which does not need to be Iris-based at all.
  • The abstract wp framework packages up sufficient conditions for an Iris program logic to be complete.
  • This version has support for languages in the Iris language hierarchy, even when they have custom weakest preconditions.
  • Completeness has been proven for the HeapLang logic (HeapLang is a language which includes unstructured concurrency, prophecy variables, and higher-order state). This allows us to start prototyping more infrastructure bridging Iris-Lean to other verification projects. If your favorite Lean framework can prove pure or stateful properties about a HeapLang program, then you will be able to import those in the context of a potentially much more complicated HeapLang proof.

Personally, I think it is extremely cool--credit going completely to the authors of the paper. Here are some ideas I want to try building off of the result:

  • Connect HeapLang to Std.do, and use it to efficiently verify simple helper functions called from a complicated concurrent host. I want to explore adding tactic support for verifying non-concurrent helper functions using symM and mvcgen, perhaps some kind of solve_by_do metaprogram.
  • Iris soundness already meant that you could use Iris as an external solver to generate pure facts that don't depend on the program state. With completeness, you can now have these proofs depend on current program state, turning knowledge about state into Iris points-to assertions. I want to see what capability Iris has for collaborative proving with automated program logics such as Loom, passing facts between the two logics in a symbiotic manner.
  • Formally exploring a RustBelt ↔ Aeneas connection. While RustBelt hasn't been ported to Lean yet, it was proven to be complete in the draft paper, and it might be possible to prototype a combined system.

I (with assistance, and vendoring some code @Sebastian Graf sent me from Lean 4.31) created a new PR which defines a new wp for single-threaded HeapLang programs and which fits into their next framework. The adequacy statement of this wp proves AdequateNoFork .NotStuck e σ Q... the precondition of the completeness theorem!

mvcgen has not been updated yet, but once it is (probably in 4.31 itself) we'll be able to use its automation for HeapLang helper functions.

Regarding release predictions: the new version of mvcgen is available as mvcgen' for now and I'm currently working on porting it to the new meta theory that would allow it to connect with deep embeddings such as HeapLang. Since the fork of 4.32 is planned for next week I cannot promise that it'll make it there, but it should become part of 4.33 and some nightly releases before that. Likely it's called just vcgen at that point.

The changes here are relatively small compared to the completeness PR though (which is what it builds on top of)
This sounds very cool! The PR is indeed a bit intimidating. Do you have a pointer to a small case study using mvcgen that one can have a look at?

Mcvgen is still only useful for monadic languages (Sebastian is generalizing it towards the language covered by this PR). Here is a tutorial about using it as it is now, ie. for shallowly embedded monadic programs

Also keep in mind that there are currently no plans in vcgen to specially support separation logic. That is, blind use will make it emit VCs such as x ↦ a ∗ y ↦ b ⊢ (x ↦ ?v) (unsat in a linear logic) instead of x ↦ a ∗ y ↦ b ⊢ (x ↦ ?v) ∗ ?F (which could be handled by a custom tactic to infer the frame).

Yes, the completeness theorem allows you to convert Iris points-tos into knowledge about a subset of your state. I'd hope that wiring this up with symM etc. so that the appropriate disjointness facts get passed down as the "initial conditions" for vcgen will be seamless!

The port of non-transfinite Iris is complete: each of the ~7250 declarations in Rocq have been accounted for in Iris-Lean.

This is a big milestone and all of the contributors to the project should be proud. I, and I'm sure I am speaking for the other maintainers as well, am personally very grateful for all of the time and effort people have contributed to the project, as it could not be done alone :heart:. I am especially thankful to the other maintainers (Michael, Zongyuan and Sergei) who have been instrumental in this final push.

Kim mentioned KLR, it is difficult for me not to reminisce about my weekends last summer: rollerblading down to the Boston Public Library and hacking together the bare minimum of stuff I'd need for work that week. I spent a long time just trying to convince people (including myself) that Iris in Lean was even possible. With this milestone, we do not need to think like that anymore.
